title: Transient splenial lesion of the corpus callosum in a case of benign convulsion associated with rotaviral gastroenteritis
case_prompt: A previously healthy 2.5-year-old girl was brought to the hospital with two brief generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She had a 2-day history of vomiting, diarrhea, and a maximum temperature of 37.8°C. The first seizure lasted 30 seconds while she was crying at home; the second lasted 1 minute in the emergency department. Her past history included one febrile convulsion at 13 months; development was normal. On examination she was alert with mild abdominal distension and slightly hyperactive bowel sounds; neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory tests showed a leukocyte count of 5600/µL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelets 227 000/µL, sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 3.6 mEq/L, chloride 108 mEq/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, BUN 8.0 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, glucose 83 mg/dL, ammonia 21 µmol/L, and calcium 9.1 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was not performed. A rotavirus stool antigen test was positive. Electroencephalography was normal. Brain MRI performed on admission showed no abnormalities on T1-, T2-, or FLAIR-weighted images, but diffusion-weighted images demonstrated a linear area of high signal intensity in the splenium of the corpus callosum with decreased apparent diffusion coefficient values.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Typical presentation of benign convulsions with mild gastroenteritis, given the patient’s age, mild dehydration, brief repetitive seizures in the setting of gastroenteritis, unremarkable interictal EEG, and excellent prognosis — “Benign convulsions associated with mild, gastroenteritis … with patients having a full recovery with good prognosis.”  
2. Rotavirus encephalitis was considered but is less likely given the absence of encephalopathic features or altered consciousness — “Although cerebrospinal fluid was not analyzed and the possibility of rotavirus encephalitis can not be excluded entirely, our case is most consistent with benign convulsions associated with rotaviral gastroenteritis based on clinical history and findings.”  
3. Other causes of splenial lesions (ischemia, infection, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, diffuse axonal injury, multiple sclerosis, hydrocephalus, Marchiafava-Bignami disease, adrenoleukodystrophy, AIDS-dementia complex, lymphoma, epilepsy, and antiepileptic drug usage) were considered but lack supporting clinical or historical evidence — “The differential diagnosis for lesions involving the SCC include ischemia, infection, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, diffuse axonal injury, multiple sclerosis, hydrocephalus, Marchiafava-Bignami disease, adrenoleukodystrophy, AIDS-dementia complex, lymphoma, epilepsy, and antiepileptic drug usage.”  
4. Splenial lesion solely from seizure propagation or antiepileptic drug effect is unlikely, as no anticonvulsants were given and interictal EEG was normal — “Splenial lesions after seizures have been reported in patients with epilepsy … no anticonvulsants were administered.”
